Armed Conflict & Security
• A powerful explosion near the Acropolis destroyed an Athens building, killing at least two; US tourists and a UK national are among the missing, as authorities probe the cause.
• Renewed clashes between Tigray forces and Ethiopia’s national army risk reigniting wider conflict, with analysts warning of a fragile political and humanitarian landscape.
• Security researchers report a surge in “LLM-jacking,” where hackers hijack companies’ AI accounts and compute, as consumers face a wave of convincing scareware via online ads.
Why it matters: From urban blasts to escalating regional wars and rising cyber exploitation of AI resources, global security threats are diversifying across physical and digital fronts.

Climate & Environment
• Bangkok declared a disaster across the capital after nearly 48 hours of rain submerged roads and canals; millions in the US Northeast also brace for an unusually powerful storm.
• Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest winter maximum on record, adding to concerns about rapid polar change.
• Wildfires in Borneo are intensifying pressure on critically endangered orangutans, while conservation programs in Guatemala and Chad highlight both gains and ongoing risks for vulnerable species.
• Regulators and policymakers stepped up actions: New Jersey levied a record fine on a datacenter for unpermitted generators; fresh disclosures reignited debate over paraquat’s safety; and a new US order prioritizing recreational fishing drew warnings from advocates.
• EV transition headwinds persist: most top-selling UK plug-in hybrids can’t use rapid chargers; US solar growth shows signs of cooling even as renewables meet rising demand.
Why it matters: Extreme weather, biodiversity strain, and regulatory battles underscore how climate risks and energy transitions are reshaping cities, industries, and ecosystems.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Iran proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz under a seven-day ceasefire via Qatari mediation; reports suggest President Trump rejected the plan, with further strikes possible after US midterms, while Washington says “constructive discussions” are ongoing.
• Trump and Xi struck a cordial tone at a summit that included top tech leaders; the US says a bilateral AI “communication channel” will open to manage incidents.
• The White House barred CNN from traveling with Trump on Air Force One for a Tennessee trip, intensifying press-access tensions.
• An Israeli ban on Arab parties ahead of elections sparked criticism as other sanctioned politicians remain eligible.
• A US appeals court upheld the Pentagon’s designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk; San Marino became the 76th signatory of NASA’s Artemis Accords.
Why it matters: From Gulf waterways to AI guardrails and media freedoms, major-power diplomacy and domestic politics are intersecting in ways that could reshape global security and norms.

• The Smithsonian’s outgoing chief defended the institution’s role in confronting difficult history amid political attacks, earning a standing ovation.
• A UK review will propose fast-tracking benefits for severely disabled youths to reduce repeated assessments; a BA cabin crew veteran’s legal fight highlights pandemic-era labor grievances.
• Pro-Palestine activism continues to roil culture and sport, with demonstrations planned at the UK Labour conference and calls to boycott an Ireland–Israel match in Hungary.

• Microsoft unveiled a consolidated Copilot app bundling chat, coding, and agent functions as it seeks an edge in enterprise AI.
• Sony and Universal sued Suno again, alleging its latest music model leverages outputs trained on unlicensed content.
• Chinese AI models have surged in global adoption, raising policy alarms in Washington over dependencies and standards.
Why it matters: As AI rapidly diffuses, safety lapses, legal battles, and geopolitical competition are shaping who sets the rules and captures value in a foundational technology.

Climate & Environment.title: Revealed: the undisclosed safety data emerging as weedkiller maker faces Parkinson’s lawsuits in US
Climate & Environment.text: Syngenta denies keeping relevant data from the EPA as paraquat stays in the US market despite global bansSweden started ringing the alarm bell more than 20 years ago, calling for a ban on the weedkilling chemical paraquat in 2004. One by one, dozens of other countries did the same as evidence of paraquat risks to human health mounted. Even the Chinese government, which owns the longtime paraquat maker Syngenta, halted domestic use of the pesticide a decade ago after conducting its own studies on paraquat safety and finding troubling results.In the US, two states – Vermont and California – have recently also banned paraquat, citing risks that include an association between paraquat and Parkinson’s disease shown in years of scientific research. And California regulators announced in August that paraquat makers voluntarily agreed to stop selling the chemical after the state identified health concerns in connection with its use in new research. Several federal lawmakers have pushed for a nationwide ban. Continue reading...

Society & Human Rights.title: Social Media Bans Aren’t Enough to Make Children Safe
Society & Human Rights.text: Even before France approved legislation banning social media for children under 15 last January, 13-year-old Benjamin was already wondering what life without social media would look like. “If we want to play football, we won’t be able to organize it. What will we do? Send letters instead?” he joked in an interview for Le Monde. His reaction captured the central challenge behind the growing wave of youth social media bans: Removing access is one thing; understanding what those platforms mean in children’s lives is another. Within weeks of Australia’s similar ban, the country’s eSafety Commissioner reported that platforms had restricted access to 4.7 million under-16 accounts. Two months later, though, one in five Australian teenagers under 16 was still using TikTok and Snapchat, according to a parental-control data company. But even if all children’s social media accounts were to disappear, do such bans actually make children safer online?Governments are moving ahead without answering that question as they follow Australia’s lead. Indonesia’s child-safety framework, which took effect in March, bars children under 16 from holding accounts on “high-risk” platforms. The U.K. government has announced  plans to ban social media for under-16s, add default overnight social media curfews for 16- and 17-year-olds, and extend child-safety rules to cover risky AI features. And on 17 September, the European Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act, which would bar children under 13 from social media, set 15 as the EU-wide minimum age for opening an account independently, and require platforms to show that their services are age appropriate and safe by design.But based on my experience working on  Child Online Protection initiatives with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) across Southeast Asia and the Pacific, I know the bans don’t address the real problems. Instead, we should be paying more attention to the systems that generate harm in the first place—namely, recommender algorithms, engagement-maximizing design, opaque moderation, and extractive data practices.Account removals are not the same as online child safetyMy experience working on protecting children’s online safety has taught me three main lessons: First, the public institutions responsible for child online protection often lack the staff, budget, or technical capacity to enforce complex online safety policies. Indonesia is illustrative. A 2026 UNICEF evaluation found capacity constraints among service providers, long-term funding uncertainty, and a need for specialized personnel. At the local level, some staff lacked digital skills, while budget constraints left some areas reliant on external support. Second, many children, and often their parents, lack the digital literacy and critical thinking skills needed to navigate online risks safely. My policy research on child online protection in Indonesia, published earlier this year in Digital Society, found substantial gaps that account removals cannot repair: Many children lacked guidance on navigating the internet safely, and large numbers did not know how to report harmful experiences. And third, the platforms have limited independent oversight as they identify underage users, design age-verification systems, and report their own compliance. In Indonesia, platforms themselves are responsible for carrying out age verification, while the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs oversees compliance. TikTok’s appeals process for users flagged as underage, for instance, can require a government-issued ID and selfies, which is a problem because it involves collecting the additional personal data on an ID card, beyond that needed to confirm age. Will government regulators ensure that TikTok handles that data responsibly? The privacy paradox of proving ageEvery age-based ban creates an engineering problem: How can a platform reliably determine that a user is old enough, without intruding on other information? Governments and companies may use identity documents, parental authorization, app-store checks, or facial age estimation. Each approach has trade-offs among accuracy, privacy, accessibility, and resistance to circumvention. There are also technical issues. One tool, facial age estimation, draws on enormous databases but it is probabilistic, not exact, because people vary so much. It’s also been shown to misclassify both children and adults. The challenge should not merely be to “verify age.” It should be to prove that someone is above a threshold, without disclosing their identity, birth date, or other information third parties might use to create a marketing profile. The European Commission’s age-verification blueprint challenges companies to verify ages without collecting all that additional information.Privacy-preserving technologies offer promising ways to achieve this. Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) can confirm that someone meets an age threshold without revealing their identity or exact date of birth. W3C Verifiable Credentials are cryptographically verifiable digital claims that can disclose only the information needed, such as “over 16.” And device-based age signals can allow a phone or app store to share an age range without revealing a user’s exact birth date. But these methods still require rigorous security testing, common standards, independent oversight, and clear limits on data retention. Otherwise, poorly designed child-safety policies risk creating permanent identity infrastructures in which businesses, not people, control personal data.Where connection goes when a platform closesBlocking access to a platform redirects some young people, but not always where expected. Early anecdotal reports in Australia pointed to teenagers migrating to smaller, less-regulated platforms like Yope, a pattern the Cato Institute flagged as a “whack-a-mole” problem for regulators. But industry data collected two months later found no broad-based shift of that kind, aside from a small uptick in WhatsApp use. Many teens simply found a way to stay on the banned platforms.This points to a deeper gap in current society: the erosion of youth “third places“ physical spaces where young people have room to socialize and build identity outside home and school. As those spaces have diminished, commercial communications platforms have absorbed that role. For many teenagers, social media workarounds are merely inconvenient. But for isolated, marginalized, disabled, or LGBTQ+ youth who depend on online communities for support that’s otherwise unavailable, displacement can mean losing certain kinds of belonging, or having to move to a platform with even weaker oversight. How to design safer online systems for childrenIf blanket social media bans don’t work, then what will? The platforms have created many of the conditions that governments are now trying to contain: engagement-optimized recommenders, intrusive data practices, weak safeguards against unwanted contact, and features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks, and persistent notifications. These design patterns increasingly face regulatory scrutiny, including what’s required under the European Union’s Digital Services Act. A 2026 study from the 5Rights Foundation that tracked children’s device use minute by minute found that the user interfaces shape children’s attention, sleep, and well-being in real time. A more durable response would regulate those interfaces directly, treating children as legitimate users whose privacy, agency, and well-being are required protections, not afterthoughts. That means designing for safety from the outset. One example would be for children’s apps to have high-privacy defaults, such as private accounts and location sharing switched off for minors. They could also have recommender systems that explain the main factors shaping a feed and give young users more control over personalization. The European Commission has published age-appropriate interaction guidelines that limit unsolicited contact and prevent minors from being added to groups without consent. Rules could also prohibit engagement-maximizing features that demand users’ attention, such as autoplay, infinite scroll, usage streaks, read receipts, and push notifications, by disabling or limiting them by default.Governments should define measurable outcomes and fund independent evaluation, platforms should give researchers meaningful data access, and engineers should audit age-assurance systems for bias and data leakage. Schools, parents, and children themselves need a seat in designing the technology that’s designed to protect children. If policymakers still decide to remove an infrastructure for youth connection, they should offer something better in return. Social media bans may reduce some forms of exposure to harmful content and may be justified for particular ages, services, or risks. But they are just one tool, not a comprehensive substitute for safer design, accountable platforms, digital literacy, institutional capacity, and noncommercial digital “third places”—moderated communities, creative spaces, and public-interest platforms designed for youth participation rather than profit.The first wave of social media restrictions isn’t enough to keep children safe. Governments are still measuring what’s easiest to count, while neglecting harder-to-measure outcomes such as children’s access to safe third places and meaningful social connection, both online and offline. Until governments can show evidence that harm has actually declined, they will keep mistaking account removal for safety.

Art & Culture.title: Off-White's "10x10: Icons Reimagined" Comes to Life at Milan's "Imaginary Palace"
Art & Culture.text: SummaryOff-White™'s "10x10: Icons Reimagined" project invited 10 global creatives to reinterpret 10 iconic Off-White pieces, culminating in the "IMAGINARY PALACE" exhibition during Milan Fashion Week.The exhibition ran from September 23–24 at Off-White's Milan space, showcasing final pieces alongside their creative references and process.Off-White™ unveiled its “10x10: Icons Reimagined” project with “IMAGINARY PALACE," a two-day exhibition during Milan Fashion Week, illuminating the exponential potential of creative collaboration. The “10x10: Icons Reimagined” project manifested earlier this year, inviting 10 global creative forces to approach 10 of its most recognizable icons as blank canvases — starting points for personal interpretation, experimentation, and rebellion. From musicians Scott Mescudi and A$AP Nast to designers Ava Nirui, Yuta Hosokawa, Raul Lopez, and Guillermo Andrade to multidisciplinary creatives Renell Medrano, Veneda Carter, Stéphane Ashpool, and Bafic, every 10x10 creator committed to following their personal vision, hacking the system, and taking their icon into the future by questioning everything. Spanning different disciplines, perspectives, and communities, the project replaced fixed rules with individual points of view. The resulting works are not homages, but continuations, opening the Off-White™ archive to transformation, allowing its legacy to evolve through the voices shaping culture and design today.Grammy Award-winning musician and fashion designer Scott Mescudi returns the "Out Of Office” sneaker to its sport codes while proposing the product as a platform — embracing use, movement, and freedom of expression. Photographer and director Renell Medrano applies her distinct perspective to new eyewear, turning her blank canvas into an investigation of looking, being seen, and perspective. Fashion designer and creative director Ava Nirui transforms the T-shirt, bringing her signature gender-neutral viewpoint and ’90s youth culture nostalgia to an everyday Off-White™ uniform and a social platform for identity, belonging, and community. 424’s designer and founder Guillermo Andrade approaches denim as an archive of memory, construction, and what came before — pairing his deep design expertise with the concept of Virgil as the muse. Designer and stylist Veneda Carter reconceptualizes Off-White’s “METEOR” motif as a visual reference, exploring the relationship between absence, form, and the body. Meanwhile, Readymade founder and designer Yuta Hosokawa reconstructs the hoodie through layers, proportions, and traces of its previous identity. Photographer, director, and multi-disciplinary artist Bafic takes Off-White’s founding space between black and white into the realm of lived experience, gathering reflections on our younger selves. Luar founder and creative director Raul Lopez shifts the Off-White™ Jitney bag through scale, shape, and perspective, weaving the philosophies of New York City and the Dominican Republic that he explores in his fashion brand’s boundary-breaking designs. French fashion designer and creative director Stéphane Ashpool repositions the familiar codes of the varsity jacket, using his unorthodox approach from his Parisian fashion label and retailer Pigalle to demonstrate how a change in perspective can transform what we think we know. Multi-hyphenate A$AP Mob member A$AP Nast reconstructs the clock to question time itself, focusing on how it is experienced rather than how it is measured — paying homage to Virgil’s ability to bend time and be everywhere at once.Across 10 individual rooms, from September 23rd to the 24th, at Off-White™’s Milan home at Via Orobia 13, the final “10x10: Icons Reimagined” objects coexist with references, materials, and the environments that led to their creation. Together with conversations and interactive workshops, the exhibition invited visitors not only to see the work, but to enter the distinct creative universes behind them. 10 creatives, 10 icons, and 10 interpretations became a potent reminder that the Off-White legacy is conceived not as something fixed, but as material for what comes next.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Nike Opens Its Massive Archive at New York’s Museum of Arts and Design
Art & Culture.text: Summary“Nike: Form Follows Motion” traces the brand from early running experiments to Air, Flyknit and Vaporfly.Archival prototypes, sketches and cultural ephemera show how Nike sneakers moved from performance tools into music, fashion and street culture.Before the Swoosh became shorthand, there were sketches, prototypes and plenty of trial and error. “Nike: Form Follows Motion,” now on view at New York’s Museum of Arts and Design, looks back at more than 50 years of the brand, from Bill Bowerman’s early waffle-sole experiments to Air Max, Jordans, Flyknit and Vaporfly. Originally organized by the Vitra Design Museum, the show pulls from Nike’s internal archive of more than 200,000 objects.Waffle Trainers, Air Force 1s, Air Jordans and Vaporflys all make an appearance, but there’s more to look at than the familiar footwear hits we've written so much about. Early samples, prototypes, sketches and old testing equipment show how some of these ideas actually started, often looking pretty far removed from the finished products we know now.The exhibition starts with Nike’s running roots before moving into the Air era. Frank Rudy’s early testing machine and air-bag prototypes are here, alongside material tracing Nike’s expansion into basketball, tennis, football and skateboarding. Michael Jordan, Serena Williams and LeBron James appear throughout, as do its legendary designers including Tinker Hatfield, Diane Katz and Eric Avar.Things get a little more technical from there. Nike Free, Flyknit and Vaporfly lead into the brand’s work around biomechanics, material research and the Nike Sport Research Lab. It’s a side of Nike that tends to get buried underneath the bigger cultural moments, but it explains a lot about how the shoes ended up looking the way they do.And for the last part of the show, it moves further away from pure performance and into the wider cultural domain. Fifty footwear examples sit alongside music videos, collaborations and other material tracing Nike through streetwear, fashion, music and sneaker cosigns. The Air Force 1, for example, became inseparable from hip-hop, while the Dunk found another life through skateboarding long after its basketball origins. Some sneakers became important for reasons that had very little to do with what they were originally designed for.The best parts of "Form Follows Motion" are probably the unfinished ones. The weird prototypes, old sketches and technical experiments offer a better look at Nike than another lineup of famous sneakers. You get to see some of the thinking before shoes became Swoosh icons.“Nike: Form Follows Motion” is on view at the Museum of Arts and Design in New York through March 7, 2027.Museum of Arts and Design2 Columbus CircleNew York, NY 10019Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Dressed in a "College Grey" and "Pink Glaze" colorway, the upper is constructed from tactile shaggy suede across the toe boxes, quarter panels, Swooshes, and tongue. Soft pink accents frame the Swoosh branding, midsole, and translucent rubber outsole, while a thin pink strip extends from the back of the heel to mimic a rat tail.Nodding directly to NYC subculture, the back of the tongue features embroidered "NYC" lettering intersected by a small Swoosh, while placing the insoles side by side forms a full slice of pizza. Entertainment.title: The URBAN RESEARCH DOORS x New Era 9THIRTY Is All About the Corduroy
Entertainment.text: SummaryNew Era and URBAN RESEARCH DOORS have rebuilt the 9THIRTY in fine-wale cotton corduroy with a subtle lusterThe low-profile crown and curved visor keep the silhouette clean enough for everyday wearThe cap comes in three seasonal colorways as the latest entry in DOORS' recurring New Era exclusive seriesNew Era and URBAN RESEARCH DOORS have teamed up on an exclusive 9THIRTY cap for Fall/Winter 2026, trading the usual cotton twill for fine-wale corduroy. It is the newest release in a New Era exclusive line that the Japanese label brings back each season, and this one leans on fabric and texture rather than graphics.The material carries the design. The crown and visor are made from 100 percent cotton corduroy with a tight, narrow wale, so the ribbing sits flat and reads closer to a refined texture than a rugged one. The pile has a soft sheen that catches the light, which gives the cap more depth than a matte fabric and more warmth for colder months. The embroidery uses polyester thread.Underneath is the 9THIRTY, New Era's unstructured-feel dad cap block. The DOORS version keeps its shallow crown and pre-curved brim, a lower, rounder shape that sits closer to the head than New Era's taller fitted profiles. The pattern is the familiar one. The fabric is what changes the character of the cap.The cap comes in one size, fitting head circumferences from 55 to 58 centimeters, with a 14-centimeter crown height and a seven-centimeter brim. The three colorways are black, brown and navy, all muted tones that suit the seasonal fabric and work equally well with casual layers or tailored outerwear.The New Era x URBAN RESEARCH DOORS 9THIRTY Corduroy is available to pre-order now via the URBAN RESEARCH online store, with delivery scheduled for early October 2026.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The LOEWE Double L Loafer Makes Its Logo Part of the Leather
Entertainment.text: Name: LOEWE Double L LoaferColorway: Black, Dark Chocolate, Deep Purple, Caramel LatteSKU: LOVL290X03-1100, LOVL290X02-9517, LOVL290X02-6417, LOVL290X02-0315MSRP: $1,150 USDRelease Date: Available nowWhere to Buy: LOEWEThe LOEWE Double L Loafer is built around softness. Its supple leather is gathered at the upper and shaped around a rounded toe, so it looks closer to a relaxed slip-on than to a stiff, structured loafer. The women's style is available in suede calfskin and soft calfskin, and every version carries the same construction details.The gathered construction defines the shoe. Rather than stretching a flat panel over a hard last, LOEWE gathers the leather across the upper, which gives the loafer soft folds and a flexible feel. The rounded toe continues that approach, avoiding the sharper profile of a traditional penny or horsebit loafer.The branding is applied in an unusual way. Instead of a metal bit or a stitched emblem, LOEWE applies its Double L signature to the upper using a high-frequency process. That keeps the logo flush with the leather and puts the focus on the material and silhouette, not on hardware.Inside and underneath, the loafer is built for comfort. A padded insole sits beneath the foot, and the shoe is fully lined in nappa leather, which is noticeably soft against the skin. The leather outsole includes a rubber island, a section of rubber set into the sole that adds grip without giving up a clean leather base. A low 10-millimeter heel keeps the profile close to the ground.The colorways split by leather. Three versions use suede calfskin: a deep Dark Chocolate, a rich Deep Purple, and a warm Caramel Latte. The fourth comes in smooth, soft calfskin in Black, the most versatile option in the range.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: thisisneverthat x Wasted Youth Recolor Visty for Fall/Winter 2026
Entertainment.text: Summarythisisneverthat and VERDY's Wasted Youth have teamed up on a Fall/Winter 2026 collection of apparel and accessoriesThe lineup is built around layering pieces, from a team jacket and light jacket to hiking pants and a check shirtA figure of Wasted Youth's signature character, Visty, comes redone in thisisneverthat's colorsthisisneverthat and Wasted Youth, the label run by graphic artist VERDY, have released a joint Fall/Winter 2026 collection. It brings the Seoul streetwear brand's cold-weather basics together with one of Japan's most recognizable graphic identities. The drop covers outerwear, trousers, and accessories, and it's anchored by a collectible figure of Visty.Outerwear leads the collection. A team jacket brings a varsity-style feel, while a lighter jacket covers the in-between weather of early fall. A check shirt fills the middle layer and can be worn alone or under either jacket. That gives the lineup a complete layering system rather than a set of standalone pieces.The hiking pants add an outdoor element. They're a practical addition for a cold-weather drop and move the collection past graphic tees and hoodies toward more functional clothing. The accessories stay practical as well. A beanie covers the colder months, and a shoulder bag keeps the essentials close.The collectible will get the most attention. The collaboration includes a figure of Visty, the character at the center of Wasted Youth's visual identity, redone in thisisneverthat's colors. It lets the collaboration reach beyond clothing and gives collectors something to display alongside the wearable pieces.The thisisneverthat x Wasted Youth collection is available now in Korea both in-store and online, and in Japan exclusively at thisisneverthat's Shibuya Flagship Store. It's also available online in the US, EU, and China.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Glenn Martens Presents Final Diesel Show & Donatella Versace Builds New Brand  in This Week's Top Fashion News
Entertainment.text: SummaryDonatella Versace joins Revolve for a 2027 brand launch; Glenn Martens leaves Diesel following his SS27 show.Jacquemus opens a Miami flagship; Dior schedules its Cruise 2028 runway for Shanghai.Nike unveils its NYC design archive; Teyana Taylor stars in Calvin Klein’s Fall campaign.Glenn Marten's Diesel SS27 Collection Was a Party About PleasureGlenn Martens concluded his transformative six-year tenure at Diesel with a spectacular send-off for the Spring/Summer 2027 season. Announced just days before the event, his departure marked the end of an era that reinvigorated the Italian denim label. Martens ensured his final runway was a memorable celebration, opening the club-inspired venue with a sensual performance art piece by the Marseille collective (LA)HORDE. The hefty 90-look collection delivered the quintessential Diesel ethos: disruptive, fluid, and fun. Highlights included inventive hybrid garments like "pantasocks," trompe l’oeil outerwear, and denim laser-cut to mimic leather. Softening the industrial edge, recurring orchid-shaped cutaways added an organic touch to the distressed fabrics. Martens’s final bow leaves behind a lasting legacy of inclusivity and pop-cultural relevance.Dontella Versace Is Launching a New BrandFollowing her departure as Chief Creative Officer of Versace in 2025, Donatella Versace is preparing her next major industry move. The Italian designer is partnering with retail giant Revolve Group to launch a brand-new fashion and beauty label in 2027. The yet-to-be-named venture aims to combine Versace's creative authority with Revolve’s expansive technological infrastructure and global reach. Revolve, which reported $1.23 billion in revenue last year, offers a massive platform for the designer to build something from scratch. Versace noted that the collaboration is rooted in a shared belief that culture stems from connection, promising a fresh voice, look, and energy. The announcement arrives in the wake of Capri Holdings’ recent $1 billion sale of Versace to the Prada Group.Dior Is Heading To Shanghai For Its Cruise 2028 ShowDior is already mapping out its long-term runway calendar, announcing that its Cruise 2028 collection will be presented in Shanghai on May 14, 2027. This move makes Dior the first major French luxury house to lock in the destination for its next resort cycle. The upcoming show marks creative director Jonathan Anderson’s first significant presentation in Asia since taking the helm last year. Shanghai holds historical weight for the brand; former director John Galliano previously staged a high-profile cruise show there in 2010. Slotted into Anderson’s dense itinerary of global destination shows—spanning Los Angeles, Paris, and Dublin—the Shanghai announcement carries added industry weight as luxury brands continue to navigate and assess the uneven market recovery across the Asian region.Teyana Taylor Brings Her Moves to Calvin Klein's Fall 2026 Underwear CampaignTeyana Taylor brought her signature swagger and dynamic energy to Calvin Klein’s Fall 2026 underwear campaign. Directed by Gordon Von Steiner, the newly launched visual spotlights the brand's Perfectly Fit Custom Lift bra through the lens of Taylor’s demanding, active lifestyle. Soundtracked to Tina Turner’s "The Best," the moody campaign video transitions from intimate reflections in a dark blue room to ecstatic, floor-work-heavy choreography in a warmly lit bedroom. Taylor emphasized that the lightweight, flexible support of the apparel allows her to move effortlessly—whether she is performing on stage, walking a red carpet, or running after her kids.Nike Opens Its Massive Archive at New York's Museum of Arts and DesignNike is pulling back the curtain on its 50-year design history with "Nike: Form Follows Motion," a new exhibition currently on view at New York's Museum of Arts and Design. Organized originally by the Vitra Design Museum, the showcase pulls from a staggering internal archive of over 200,000 objects. Instead of merely displaying familiar footwear hits, the exhibit highlights the brand's gritty trial-and-error process. Visitors can explore early waffle-sole experiments, raw prototypes, old testing equipment, and initial sketches from legendary designers like Tinker Hatfield. Moving from pure performance into broader cultural impact, the exhibit contextualizes how silhouettes like the Dunk transitioned from the hardwood to the skate park. The comprehensive retrospective remains open through March 2027, offering a rare glimpse into the unfinished thoughts behind the Swoosh.Jacquemus Opens Mediterranean-Inspired Flagship in Miami Design DistrictJacquemus has officially expanded its footprint to South Florida, opening a new brick-and-mortar flagship in the Miami Design District. Designed in collaboration with architectural firm OMA, the two-story, 2,906-square-foot space translates the French house’s Mediterranean aesthetic for the coast. The boutique features handcrafted stucco walls, warm Italian terracotta tiles by Cotto Etrusco, and a striking Saint-Marc Jaune stone staircase. Beyond retail, founder Simon Porte Jacquemus curated the space to double as a gallery, outfitting it with collectible furniture and fine art installations, including bronze sculptures and pieces by Pablo Picasso and Wolfgang Tillmans. Complete with a dedicated shoe salon and a private VIP area, the sun-drenched Miami boutique is now open to the public, blending bespoke architecture with the brand’s relaxed codes.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Jil Sander's Next PUMA Pack Strips Back the Classics
Entertainment.text: SummaryJil Sander and PUMA are releasing minimalist, stripped-back versions of the classic Speedcat and Suede sneakers for SS27.The collaboration features monochromatic colorways and slim silhouettes, though an official release date and price remain unconfirmed.Jil Sander and PUMA are returning to refresh two PUMA classics through a lens of subtraction. ⁠Previewed at the Milan Fashion Week SS27 runway show by guests like King Princess and Space Afrika, the designer label is coming out with a stripped-back variant of the PUMA Speedcat and the PUMA Suede.⁠Instead of adding to the design of the Speedcat, creative director Simone Bellotti reduces it, replacing the signature Formstrip with a perforated shadow. ⁠Other than the small, golden Jil Sander logo on the lacing system, the Black colorway is entirely monochromatic, giving the smoothly shaped silhouette a luxurious feel in full leather. Taking after the Black colorway, the White Speedcat is also completely monochromatic; however, for those who prefer the signature detail, the white colorway boasts a streamlined suede Formstrip for variety. The new Jil Sander x Speedcat is also joined by a white Jil Sander x PUMA Suede, featuring tonal details to complete the lineup.⁠The partners' latest collaboration takes after the SS26 Jil Sander x PUMA K-Street, which dialled in on the slim-sneaker trend. "In recent years, the slim silhouette has become very fashionable again, but I’m not someone who really follows fashion; it’s something I have always liked," he said in an April interview with Hypebeast. "I’m not a huge fan of the big, chunky silhouettes. A very slim silhouette feels more “pure” in a way; it goes to the essence of the meaning of a shoe, without having too much design or material over it," he added.As of the time of writing, Jil Sander nor PUMA has confirmed the official release date or retail price.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Toyota Prepares Us for Moon Festival With Its Curated Starter Packs
Entertainment.text: Mid-Autumn calls for good company under a full moon, so we've teamed up with Toyota to curate three ways to celebrate – each paired with the vehicle built to get you there. Whether the plan is an intimate dinner at home, a rooftop gathering with friends, or a drive out to the water for moonrise, these Starter Packs make sure you arrive ready.Toyota bZ – “The Urbanite” Moon Festival Starter PackFor the Toyota bZ's quiet, city-ready glide, The Urbanite’s night revolves around a dinner that quietly becomes a moon-viewing, without anyone needing to leave the table. The idea is intentional rather than elaborate — good tea, a few sweets, and a lantern doing most of the work once everyone drifts toward the balcony. It’s a gathering built to fit however many square feet you’ve got, structured around ritual rather than production.What's inside:Set the table with a snow-skin mooncake keepsake box from Man Fu Yuan.A pot of osmanthus oolong by Harney & Sons, poured from the KINTO “Leaves to Tea” teapot and cup set.Keep the leaves fresh between pours with a Kaikado copper tea caddy.Candied osmanthus sweets and traditional mooncakes travel out to the balcony in a Hasami Porcelain stacking set.Once outside, a Noguchi Akari paper lantern takes over the lighting.Round out the atmosphere with APFR incense and a brass holder.When the moon climbs higher, break out a vintage mahjong set to keep hands busy while everyone watches the sky.Toyota C-HR – "The Performer" Moon Festival Starter PackThe Toyota C-HR’s sharp, city-quick handling makes it the natural fit for The Performer’s rooftop take on Mid-Autumn, where a moon-viewing turns a bare roof into a venue everyone’s actually excited to be at. This one runs loud and late, built less around a sit-down dinner and more around a rotating cast of drinks, music, and whoever shows up next. The goal isn’t about stillness — it’s about keeping the night moving until well past moonrise.What's inside:Set the tone for the night with a Teenage Engineering OB-4.A Wooj lantern's sculpted silhouette does as much for the space as the light it casts.Keep a Polaroid Now in rotation for capturing the night as it unfolds.Snow Peak's Ti-Double stacking cups get passed around for rounds of Ghia's “Le Spritz.”A portable karaoke mic and a Pocha table keep the group circulating.Cover the concrete with a packable roof blanket.Throw whatever's queued up against the nearest wall with a video projector.Modern mooncakes and a rotating dessert spread stay out for the duration.Toyota bZ Woodland – “The Explorer” Moon Festival Starter PackThe Toyota bZ Woodland’s rugged, trail-ready capability sets up The Explorer’s version of Mid-Autumn — a drive out to a waterfront basecamp, built around the long wait that moonrise actually rewards. There’s no rushing this one; the whole point is settling in early and letting the evening unfold at its own pace. Snacks, a fire, and a few good chairs do most of the heavy lifting while the sky finishes the job.What's inside:Track the horizon with a pair of Nocs Standard Issue binoculars.A Solo Stove Mesa burns clean enough to sit close to for hours.Get dinner going with a Snow Peak Home & Camp Burner.A Titanium Kanpai flask holds roasted hojicha from Kettl through the cooler stretches.Cover the group as temperatures drop off the water with a Snow Peak x Pendleton wool blanket.Keep pomelo and shared snacks cold in a Rareform soft cooler.Helinox chairs give everyone a place to settle in.Save mooncakes — egg yolk or meat — in a Japanese jubako stacking lacquer box for the moment the moon clears the horizon.Read more at Hypebeast

The cancer research community, as is often the case when it comes to specific components of the immune system, has led the way in generating a better understanding of these cells, and so much of the present literature is focused on their role in cancer. Generally speaking, patients with more type 1 conventional dendritic cells tends to exhibit better outcomes, because the cancer will be more aggressively attacked by the immune system.
